questions.stem: Retrieval failure theory explains forgetting as:
options: deliberately pushing a distressing memory out of awareness
stored information cannot be accessed without suitable cues
the fading of a memory trace through lack of use over time
new information disrupting the retrieval of older information
questions.explanation: Retrieval failure means the information is still stored in long-term memory but cannot be accessed, usually because the right retrieval cues are absent. Fading through disuse is decay theory.

questions.stem: Jack knows the name of an actor, can say it starts with 'B' and has two syllables, but cannot produce it. This tip-of-the-tongue experience best supports:
options: motivated forgetting
retrieval failure theory
decay of the memory trace
proactive interference
questions.explanation: Jack can retrieve partial information about the name, so the memory is clearly stored. He lacks the cue needed to access the whole of it, which is retrieval failure rather than decay.

questions.stem: Ella cannot remember her Year 3 teacher's name until she walks past her old classroom, when it suddenly comes back. This shows that:
options: the memory was available but needed a cue to be accessed
the memory had decayed and was then rebuilt by the classroom
new memories had retroactively erased the teacher's name
she had repressed the memory because it was distressing
questions.explanation: Seeing the classroom provided a retrieval cue that gave access to information already stored. If the memory had decayed, a cue could not have brought it back.

questions.stem: Proactive interference occurs when:
options: old information disrupts the retrieval of new information
new information disrupts the retrieval of old information
a memory fades because it has not been used
a person consciously chooses to forget an event
questions.explanation: In proactive interference, previously learned information interferes forward in time with recalling newer information. Retroactive interference works backwards, with new learning disrupting old.

questions.stem: After moving house, Zara keeps giving her old address when asked for her new one. This is an example of:
options: proactive interference
retroactive interference
decay theory
motivated forgetting
questions.explanation: The older, well-learned address is disrupting the retrieval of the newer one, so the interference acts forwards in time. That is proactive interference.

questions.stem: After learning Japanese this year, Raj finds he can no longer remember French words he learned two years ago. This is:
options: proactive interference
retrieval failure due to state
decay of sensory memory
retroactive interference
questions.explanation: The newer learning (Japanese) is interfering with the retrieval of older learning (French). When new information disrupts old information, it is retroactive interference.

questions.stem: Group A learns List 1 then List 2; Group B learns List 1 then rests. Both recall List 1. Group A recalls less. The result demonstrates:
options: retroactive interference, because List 2 disrupted recall of List 1
proactive interference, because List 1 disrupted recall of List 2
decay theory, because Group A waited longer before recall
motivated forgetting, because Group A disliked List 1
questions.explanation: Both groups were tested on the older list, and only the group that learned new material in between recalled less. New learning disrupting old learning is retroactive interference.

questions.stem: Interference is most likely to cause forgetting when the two sets of information are:
options: learned many years apart in different places
similar to each other, such as two lists of words
very different, such as a phone number and a dance step
both processed deeply for their meaning
questions.explanation: Interference is strongest when the competing material is similar, because the memories are easily confused at retrieval. Dissimilar material produces little interference.

questions.stem: Motivated forgetting refers to forgetting that:
options: occurs because similar information competes at retrieval
occurs because retrieval cues are missing at the time of testing
occurs because a memory trace weakens with time
occurs because a person wants to avoid a distressing memory
questions.explanation: Motivated forgetting occurs when there is a conscious or unconscious desire to forget, usually because a memory is painful or threatening. The other options describe interference, retrieval failure and decay.

questions.stem: How does repression differ from suppression?
options: Repression affects only short-term memory; suppression affects only LTM
Repression is caused by head injury; suppression by alcohol use
Repression is unconscious; suppression is a conscious effort to forget
Repression is conscious; suppression happens without awareness
questions.explanation: Repression is an unconscious process that blocks a distressing memory from awareness. Suppression is a deliberate, conscious attempt to push a memory out of mind.

questions.stem: A woman who was not physically hurt in a frightening car accident cannot remember it, but becomes very distressed when she later drives past the site. Which type of forgetting does this most likely show?
options: decay of the memory trace through disuse
retroactive interference from later events
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
motivated forgetting through repression
questions.explanation: The memory appears blocked from awareness yet still affects her emotions, which suggests it is stored but repressed because it is threatening. A decayed memory would not trigger such a reaction.

questions.stem: Decay theory proposes that forgetting occurs because:
options: the memory trace fades when it is not used over time
new memories overwrite older memories in the same store
the right retrieval cues are absent when trying to recall
a person is motivated to forget unpleasant events
questions.explanation: Decay theory proposes that a memory trace gradually weakens and disappears through disuse. It explains forgetting from the sensory register and short-term memory better than from long-term memory.

questions.stem: Which finding is the strongest challenge to decay theory as an explanation of long-term forgetting?
options: Information in short-term memory is lost within about 30 seconds
Visual sensory information fades within a fraction of a second
Older people often report more trouble remembering names
Unused memories from decades ago can be recalled with the right cue
questions.explanation: If unused memories can be recalled years later when a cue is given, they cannot have faded away. Rapid loss from the sensory register and short-term memory fits decay theory rather than challenging it.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to test decay theory but finds it hard to design a fair study. The main reason is that:
options: participants always remember more after a longer delay
decay theory makes no prediction about the passage of time
it is hard to stop new learning, and so interference, during the delay
decay can only be measured in the sensory register, not in long-term memory
questions.explanation: To test decay, nothing else should happen between learning and recall, but people keep experiencing new information. Any forgetting could then be due to interference rather than decay.

questions.stem: Kai looks up a word, is distracted by a text message, and seconds later cannot recall the word. Which explanation fits best?
options: proactive interference from earlier long-term memories
damage to the hippocampus
decay from short-term memory before rehearsal
motivated forgetting of a threatening word
questions.explanation: Information not rehearsed in short-term memory is quickly lost, and the distraction stopped him rehearsing it. There is no reason to want to forget the word, and no similar earlier learning to interfere with it.

questions.stem: Which statement about decay theory is most accurate?
options: It explains loss from long-term memory better than from short-term memory
It states that forgetting happens because retrieval cues are missing
It states that similar memories compete with each other at retrieval
It explains loss from sensory and short-term memory better than from LTM
questions.explanation: Information in the sensory register and short-term memory fades quickly without attention or rehearsal, which fits decay. Long-term memories can resurface after years of disuse, which decay theory struggles to explain.

questions.stem: Chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) is a form of memory loss caused by:
options: a genetic disorder that appears only in childhood
a single episode of severe emotional stress
repeated blows to the head, such as in contact sport
a lack of thiamine, often linked to chronic alcohol use
questions.explanation: CTE is a progressive brain disease linked to repeated head impacts, including concussions and smaller blows that do not cause symptoms at the time. A lack of thiamine causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.stem: In CTE, the brain shows abnormal build-up of which protein?
options: insulin
myelin
haemoglobin
tau
questions.explanation: CTE involves the abnormal build-up of tau protein in the brain, which damages neurons over time. Tau is also found in the neurofibrillary tangles of Alzheimer's disease.

questions.stem: A former professional footballer, now in his 50s, has memory problems, poor impulse control, sudden aggression and depression. These symptoms are most consistent with:
options: chronic traumatic encephalopathy
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
decay of sensory memory
a single mild concussion last week
questions.explanation: Memory loss together with impulsivity, aggression and mood changes, years after a career of repeated head impacts, is consistent with CTE. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is linked to thiamine deficiency.

questions.stem: Why is it difficult to study CTE in living people?
options: Its symptoms always appear within days of the injury
It can currently be confirmed only by examining the brain after death
It produces no changes in behaviour or emotion while the person is alive
It affects only people who have had a single severe head injury
questions.explanation: A definitive diagnosis of CTE currently requires examining brain tissue after death. This means researchers often rely on retrospective case studies of donated brains.

questions.stem: Which statement about the symptoms of CTE is correct?
options: They improve steadily once the person stops playing sport
They affect only movement and never mood or memory
They often appear years after the repeated head impacts
They always appear within a day of the first concussion
questions.explanation: CTE is progressive, and symptoms such as memory loss, mood changes and poor judgement often emerge years or decades after the head impacts. They tend to worsen rather than improve over time.

questions.stem: Alzheimer's disease is classified as which cause of memory loss?
options: drug-induced
motivated forgetting
degeneration
trauma
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disease in which neurons are gradually damaged and die. CTE is linked to trauma and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is drug-induced.

questions.stem: Which pair of brain changes is characteristic of Alzheimer's disease?
options: amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles
a lack of thiamine and damage to mammillary bodies
an enlarged hippocampus and extra neurons
a build-up of myelin and loss of tau
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease is marked by beta-amyloid plaques between neurons and neurofibrillary tangles of tau protein inside them. Thiamine deficiency and damage to the mammillary bodies describe Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.stem: In the early stage of Alzheimer's disease, a person is most likely to have difficulty:
options: riding a bike they rode as a child
recognising every family member
speaking in full sentences
remembering recent events
questions.explanation: The hippocampus is affected early, so forming new explicit memories is often the first difficulty. Well-learned procedural skills tend to be preserved until much later in the disease.

questions.stem: Why are procedural memories often preserved longer than recent explicit memories in Alzheimer's disease?
options: Amyloid plaques form first in the cerebellum
Explicit memories are stored in the sensory register
The cerebellum is affected later than the hippocampus
Procedural memories are stored in the hippocampus
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease damages the hippocampus and nearby areas early, impairing new explicit memories. The cerebellum, involved in implicit procedural memories, is affected later in the disease.

questions.stem: Besides memory loss, which impact on behaviour and emotion is common as Alzheimer's disease progresses?
options: improved concentration and planning
greater interest in new hobbies
faster reaction times
mood changes, anxiety and agitation
questions.explanation: As the disease progresses, people often experience mood swings, anxiety, irritability, agitation and withdrawal. These come from damage to brain areas involved in emotion and from the distress of memory loss.

questions.stem: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is caused by a deficiency of:
options: vitamin D (calciferol)
vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
iron and folate
thiamine (vitamin B1)
questions.explanation: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency, most commonly linked to chronic heavy alcohol use, which reduces the intake and absorption of thiamine.

questions.stem: Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is classified as drug-induced memory loss because:
options: it is caused by medication for epilepsy
it is most often linked to long-term heavy alcohol use
it is caused by repeated concussions in contact sport
it results from inherited changes to brain proteins
questions.explanation: Chronic heavy alcohol use is the most common cause of the thiamine deficiency behind Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Repeated concussions are linked to CTE.

questions.stem: Wernicke's encephalopathy, the first phase of WKS, typically involves:
options: rapid improvement in memory after a period of rest
confusion, poor coordination and abnormal eye movements
slow loss of procedural memory over several decades of life
vivid flashbacks and a heightened startle response
questions.explanation: Wernicke's encephalopathy is an acute phase marked by confusion, poor muscle coordination (ataxia) and abnormal eye movements. If untreated it can lead to Korsakoff syndrome.

questions.stem: A man with a long history of heavy drinking cannot remember what he did this morning and gives detailed but false accounts of his day without meaning to deceive. This false recall is called:
options: elaborative rehearsal
confabulation
repression
proactive interference
questions.explanation: Confabulation is producing false memories without intending to lie, and it is a feature of Korsakoff syndrome. It fills the gaps left by severe anterograde amnesia.

questions.stem: The main memory impairment in Korsakoff syndrome is:
options: severe difficulty forming new memories
loss of only procedural memories
loss of only sensory memory
improved recall of old memories
questions.explanation: Korsakoff syndrome causes severe anterograde amnesia, so new memories are not formed, along with some loss of older memories. Procedural skills are relatively spared.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares CTE and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome?
options: CTE results from repeated head trauma; WKS from thiamine deficiency
CTE results from thiamine deficiency; WKS from repeated head trauma
Both are caused mainly by inherited changes to tau protein
Both are caused by the fading of memory traces through disuse
questions.explanation: CTE is trauma-related memory loss from repeated head impacts, while WKS is drug-induced memory loss from thiamine deficiency, usually linked to alcohol. Their causes are very different.

questions.stem: Early treatment with thiamine is important in Wernicke's encephalopathy because:
options: it restores memories that were repressed after a traumatic event
it can ease symptoms and stop progression to Korsakoff syndrome
it reverses all of the amyloid plaques and tangles in the brain
it removes tau protein that built up from repeated head impacts
questions.explanation: Giving thiamine early can improve the acute symptoms and help prevent the lasting memory damage of Korsakoff syndrome. Plaques, tangles and tau build-up belong to other conditions.

questions.stem: Which cause of memory loss is matched to its category correctly?
options: CTE - trauma
Alzheimer's disease - drug-induced
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome - degeneration
CTE - degeneration only, with no injury involved
questions.explanation: CTE is caused by trauma (repeated head impacts). Alzheimer's disease is degenerative and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is drug-induced.

questions.stem: Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after the onset of a condition. Which conditions commonly produce it?
options: decay of iconic memory and retrieval failure
maintenance and elaborative rehearsal
proactive and retroactive interference
Alzheimer's disease and Korsakoff syndrome
questions.explanation: Both Alzheimer's disease and Korsakoff syndrome damage structures needed to form new explicit memories, so anterograde amnesia is common. The other options are explanations of everyday forgetting or memory strategies, not conditions.

questions.stem: Studying similar subjects back to back, such as Spanish then Italian, is likely to increase forgetting through:
options: interference
decay
motivated forgetting
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome
questions.explanation: Similar material learned close together is easily confused at retrieval, so interference increases. Separating similar subjects with dissimilar ones can reduce it.
